common_name: Amazonian Zebra Plant (Chantinii Bromeliad, Zebra Aechmea)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded, frost-free patio container; Amazonian Zebra Plant is one of the more cold-sensitive bromeliads and suffers damage below 45°F, so bring containers indoors well before frost outside zone 10-11. Pot in a coarse, fast-draining orchid-bark mix and keep the central cup topped off with rainwater or distilled water. Divide and pot up rooted offsets (pups) once they reach roughly one-third the size of the parent.

directions: Provide bright, filtered light — more light than most tank bromeliads tolerate is needed to bring out the bold banding, but direct midday sun will scorch the leaves, so an east-facing window or high-canopy shade outdoors is ideal. Aechmea chantinii is a large epiphytic bromeliad from the Amazon basin of Peru, Brazil, Colombia, and Ecuador, prized for broad, arching leaves marked with alternating horizontal bands of silver-gray and deep green that give the plant its 'zebra' common name; leaf margins carry small dark spines, so site it away from foot traffic. After several years of growth the rosette sends up a dramatic, multi-tiered flower spike of red-orange bracts holding small yellow-and-red flowers, followed by long-lasting berries. Keep the central water-holding cup flushed with fresh water every few weeks to prevent stagnation, and expect the mother rosette to die back naturally after flowering as pups take over.

common_name: King of Bromeliads (Hieroglyphic Vriesea, Painted Feather)

planting.note: Grow as a large specimen houseplant or shaded conservatory/patio container in zone 10-11; King of Bromeliads has no frost tolerance and needs consistent warmth (60°F minimum) and high humidity year-round. Pot in a loose, well-draining bark-and-perlite mix over a wide, shallow container since the root system is modest relative to the rosette's size. Because the plant is slow to reach blooming size, most home growers acquire it as an established juvenile rather than starting from a small pup.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light or dappled shade — direct sun bleaches out the dramatic leaf markings that give this species its name, while too little light produces a plain green, less patterned rosette. Vriesea hieroglyphica is a large, slow-growing epiphytic bromeliad from the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, celebrated among collectors for its broad, glossy, yellow-green leaves overlaid with irregular dark purple-brown cross-bands resembling ancient script, earning it the nickname 'King of Bromeliads.' A mature rosette can take several years to bloom, eventually producing a tall, simple, sword-like spike of yellow flowers emerging from greenish bracts; the foliage, not the bloom, is the main ornamental feature. Keep the central cup filled with rainwater or distilled water, flushing it periodically, and avoid tap water high in mineral salts, which can mark the leaves.

planting.note: Plant outdoors as a groundcover in zone 10-11, or grow in shallow pots/hanging baskets elsewhere; Fireball Bromeliad has no frost tolerance and is damaged below 35°F. In warm-winter landscapes it is widely used as a mass-planted color bed under tree canopies, since it spreads quickly into a dense, self-repeating carpet as pups root beside the parent rosette. Divide and reset overcrowded clumps every 1-2 years to keep individual rosettes tight and well colored.

directions: Give bright, filtered light or a few hours of gentle morning sun — Fireball colors up brightest red with more light exposure, while deep shade fades the rosette toward green. Neoregelia 'Fireball' is a compact hybrid bromeliad, one of the most widely planted dwarf Neoregelia cultivars in Florida and Gulf Coast landscaping, forming a tight, flat rosette only a few inches across that turns a saturated wine-red to fire-engine red as it matures. It is grown almost entirely for its intense, long-lasting foliage color rather than its small, inconspicuous violet flowers, which are tucked low in the central water-holding cup and barely rise above the leaves. Because each rosette is small and shallow-rooted, it thrives tucked into rock gardens, tree crotches, mixed containers, or as a dense edging planting, and established colonies self-propagate readily from offsets. Keep the tiny central cup topped with water and avoid heavy fertilizer, which encourages green, less colorful growth.

common_name: Painted Fingernail Plant (Fingernail Bromeliad, Spectabilis Neoregelia)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or in a shaded, frost-free container garden; Painted Fingernail Plant tolerates only brief dips near 40°F and needs protection below that. Pot in a coarse, well-draining bark-based bromeliad mix, since the roots mainly serve to anchor the plant rather than take up water. Keep the central cup filled and offset the parent rosette's pups into their own pots once they have a few roots of their own.

directions: Provide bright, indirect light — stronger light intensifies the red leaf tips that give this species its common name, while low light produces an all-green rosette. Neoregelia spectabilis is a medium-sized epiphytic bromeliad native to the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, forming a broad, open rosette of stiff, olive-green to bronze strap-shaped leaves that are each tipped in vivid red, resembling a hand of freshly painted fingernails; the leaf undersides carry fine silvery-gray cross-banding. Like other Neoregelias, its true flowers are small and largely hidden within the central water-filled cup, so the plant is grown chiefly for its foliage color and form rather than its bloom. It tolerates a wider range of light than many bromeliads and adapts well to bright windowsills, making it a popular beginner species among Neoregelia collectors.

common_name: Summer Torch Bromeliad (Foolproof Plant, Pyramidal Billbergia)

planting.note: Plant outdoors in partial shade to filtered sun in zone 9b-11; Summer Torch tolerates brief drops into the upper 20s°F once established and is regularly grown as a permanent, low-maintenance groundcover under tree canopies across Florida and the Gulf Coast. In zone 9, mulch heavily over winter or grow in a container that can be moved under cover during hard freezes. Divide crowded clumps by separating rooted offsets any time during active growth.

directions: Grow in filtered sun to partial shade — Summer Torch is among the more sun-tolerant tank bromeliads and can handle a few hours of direct morning sun outdoors, though hot afternoon sun will scorch the leaves. Billbergia pyramidalis is a clump-forming bromeliad native to Brazil and the Caribbean, earning the nickname 'foolproof plant' for its tolerance of neglect, drought, and a wide range of soils and light. Its loose, vase-shaped rosettes of glossy green leaves send up a short, dense, pyramid-shaped flower head in summer, packed with brilliant scarlet-red bracts and blue-tipped petals that make it one of the showiest and easiest bromeliads to bloom reliably outdoors. Keep the central cup topped with water, but the plant also tolerates the cup drying out briefly, unlike more sensitive tank bromeliads. Established colonies spread readily by offsets and naturalize into dense drifts.

common_name: Zebra Plant Earth Star (Zoned Cryptanthus, Banded Earth Star)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, terrarium plant, or shaded container specimen in zone 10-11; Zebra Plant Earth Star has no frost tolerance and prefers steady warmth above 60°F. Unlike tank bromeliads, it has no central water cup and roots directly in a peat- or coir-based, well-draining potting mix, so water it like a typical houseplant rather than filling a cup. High humidity (50-70%) improves banding and leaf texture, making it a favorite for closed terrariums and bottle gardens.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — direct sun bleaches the banding, while too little light produces a duller, less patterned rosette. Cryptanthus zonatus is a small, flat, entirely terrestrial bromeliad native to Brazil, distinguished from its relative Cryptanthus bivittatus by wavy-margined leaves marked with irregular horizontal ('zoned') cross-bands of silvery gray on a brown-green background, rather than lengthwise stripes. The star-shaped rosette hugs the soil surface and spreads slowly by offsets that root right at the base of the parent plant, making it an excellent low groundcover in shaded terrarium plantings or mixed dish gardens. Small white flowers occasionally appear in the rosette center but are inconspicuous compared to the foliage. Because it absorbs water through its roots rather than a central cup, keep the potting mix evenly moist but never soggy.

common_name: Bird's Nest Bromeliad (Blushing Nidularium, Innocentii Bromeliad)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or in a shaded, frost-free container garden in zone 10-11; Bird's Nest Bromeliad is a rainforest-floor species with essentially no cold or frost tolerance. Pot in a loose, well-draining, humus-rich bark-and-peat mix that mimics the leaf litter it grows in naturally, and keep humidity elevated. Divide and pot up rooted offsets once they have formed several of their own leaves.

directions: Grow in medium to deep, filtered shade — Nidularium innocentii is a true forest-floor understory plant and is more shade-tolerant than most tank bromeliads, with strong light bleaching or browning the leaves. Native to the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, it forms a dense, low rosette of glossy, dark green to purplish-bronze strap leaves; at flowering time the innermost leaves flush bright red, cradling small white to lavender flowers nestled deep at the center like eggs in a nest, which gives the genus its common name. It is closely related to Neoregelia but is distinguished botanically by its floral bracts, which form a tight, layered structure around the flowers rather than lying flat. Keep the central cup filled with rainwater or distilled water and grow it on the moist side, since this species comes from consistently humid rainforest floors rather than drier epiphytic niches.

common_name: Striped Torch Bromeliad (Florida Guzmania, West Indian Tufted Airplant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, mounted epiphyte, or shaded container specimen; Striped Torch has no frost tolerance outside its native south Florida hammocks and swamps, where it grows as a protected epiphyte. It can be mounted on a piece of wood or bark like a Tillandsia, or potted in a very open, fast-draining orchid-bark mix. This species is state-listed as endangered in Florida due to habitat loss and over-collection, so only source nursery-propagated plants and never remove it from the wild.

directions: Provide bright, filtered light similar to dappled canopy shade — this species naturally grows as an epiphyte on tree limbs in humid hammocks, so it favors more airflow and slightly less constant moisture in its cup than tank-forming Guzmanias. Guzmania monostachia is native to south Florida (including Everglades and Big Cypress hammocks), the Caribbean, and Central and South America, forming a soft, arching rosette of light green, strap-shaped leaves. Its inflorescence is distinctive among Guzmanias: a slender, upright spike of white to cream bracts striped and tipped with green and, later, red, topped with small white flowers, rather than the flat colorful star of bracts typical of Guzmania lingulata. Mist occasionally and keep a small amount of water in the central cup, flushing it periodically to prevent stagnation.

planting.note: Plant outdoors in partial shade to filtered sun in zone 9b-11; Turtle Bromeliad is one of the tougher, more cold-tolerant tank bromeliads in general landscape use, handling brief dips into the upper 20s°F once established. In zone 9, site it in a protected spot or mulch heavily over winter. Divide crowded clumps by separating rooted offsets from the base of the parent rosette.

directions: Grow in filtered sun to partial shade — Quesnelia testudo tolerates more direct light than many tank bromeliads, which suits it to open shade-tree plantings rather than only deep shade. Native to the Rio de Janeiro region of Brazil, it has been in cultivation since the 1800s and forms a stiff, arching rosette of grayish-green, spine-edged strap leaves. Its common name comes from the compact, domed flower head of coral-pink bracts and blue-violet flowers, which some growers liken to the shape of a turtle's shell rising from the foliage. Keep the central cup topped with water and grow in a coarse, fast-draining bromeliad or orchid mix; established clumps are tough, forgiving, and long-lived in the landscape.
